item.title: Pingry stays perfect, topples Delbarton in boys soccer final
item.description: FRANKLIN TOWNSHIP — Ryan Miller sat on the turf at Franklin High School, shaking his head a little as Pingry head soccer coach Miller Bugliari shared kudos and his assistants waved the NJSIAA Non-Public soccer trophy in the air. The Big Blue goalkeeper had anchored a 2-0 victory against Delbarton. But "it hasn't hit me yet," he admitted, as he was pulled this way and that for photos and congratulations. Miller, a sophomore from Chatham, knew the pain from Pingry's loss to St. Benedict's Prep last fall. Junior Julian Lopez, who scored both Pingry goals, had felt that anguish twice. But this time, the Big Blue left no doubt with a perfect 25-0 season. They also captured the Somerset County Tournament and Prep A this fall. After the match, the players gathered with their fans at the far end of the field, singing Oasis' "Wonderwall." "The past two years, we've been like, 'Next year's our year,'" said Lopez, who broke Pingry's single-season (45) and career (78) goals records. "The passion to win in this game is what fueled us all year. We won everything else the previous two seasons. This was the only thing the seniors had yet to win. It feels amazing to be able to add another championship." The Big Blue had lost to St. Benedict's Prep in the Non-Public A final the past two years. Delbarton had faced the same fate one round earlier. But this year, the Green Wave took down the Gray Bees in a Non-Public A semifinal, then outlasted Seton Hall Prep on Nov. 12 to get to the overall final. Ranked third all-time with 13 NJSIAA boys soccer titles, this was Delbarton's first trip to the Non-Public A final since 2018. "There's a little bit of pressure knowing what's coming at you," said Miller, who made eight saves in the final and credited his back line of seniors Ryan Stern and Brian Anders, junior Colton Gedroic and sophomore Josh Guberuk. "But it's been great with all these boys. I just love it every day." This is Pingry's seventh Non-Public soccer title, the first since 2014 when the team was still in the small-school division. Assistant coach Dave Fahey recalled how his own Big Blue playing career had ended in the 1998 Non-Public A final against Delbarton. He pointed out that Pingry has won five straight sectional titles, and been in the final three straight times. An assistant to Bugliari since graduating from Boston University in 2003, Fahey dashed around celebrating with other alumni going as far back as the 1960s. "This is family right here," he said. "This is what it means to us." This article originally appeared on Morristown Daily Record: Pingry stays perfect, topples Delbarton in boys soccer final

item.title: Topps reveals Gem Mint 10 Lando Norris card with Coca-Cola suit patch
item.description: Motorsport photo Topps has shared one of its rarest Lando Norris cards: a signed 2024 Dynasty Formula 1 card with two pieces of race suit, one of them cut from the Coca-Cola logo on the sleeve of his McLaren race suit. The Topps Racing account posted a short video of the card on Instagram on Friday, with the caption "This Lando Norris patch auto goes CRAZY!" The card comes from the Single Driver Dual Relic Autograph set. Two windows of red fabric sit below Norris's signature. The left-hand piece shows part of the white Coca-Cola script. It has been graded by the American company PSA, which sealed it in a plastic case with its highest grade, Gem Mint 10. Fans spotted the logo straight away. "Where did they get his race suit?" asked one of the commenters under the post. "Omg this is so dope," someone else commented, while another added: "Hahaha Coca-Cola wants to come back to Spain and see the chaos that erupted over the Coca-Cola bottle. Coca-Cola, become a sponsor of LN4 Fusion!" Norris went viral after the Spanish Grand Prix at the new Madring Circuit during a moment in the cooldown room. Norris was seemingly asked to put down the Coca-Cola he was drinking, but he refused. “I just did a race, so I’m allowed to drink what I would like. Thank you so much,” Norris said at the time. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Topps Racing (@toppsracing) The moment caused chaos online as PepsiCo, a rival of Coca-Cola, is an official partner of F1. Norris was pressed further on the situation while speaking to the media in Austin, Texas. “No, no one’s ever said anything to me since. I feel like we should be allowed to drink whatever we want after a race, especially when you’re in it for two hours. "It’s been some of the hottest races, cars are also difficult to drive, so I feel like I should be allowed to drink what I want.” He added: “From a team, the team might have been told off more than I was. And therefore we have little holders to put our drinks in, so it’s unbranded, but I’m allowed to drink whatever I can. It’s just the branding issues that they have. "But this is not something I need to be thinking of, or I should be thinking of, so it’s some stuff I’m sure that was cleared up between other people. That’s simply all it was I think. It’s just TV and branding and all of those things, but I can drink whatever I like.” Dynasty is the most expensive F1 product Topps makes. Each box holds a single encased card, always an autograph with a relic, and every one is numbered to 10 copies or fewer. When the 2024 edition went on sale in February 2025, a box cost $1,099.99 . The base version of this Norris card is limited to 10 copies, with rarer red, black and gold versions on top. To read more Motorsport.com articles visit our website .

item.title: Austin Championship: Trace Crowe grabs 54-hole lead late
item.description: Trace Crowe birdied his final two holes Saturday to get to 14 under and separate himself from three other players through 54 holes of the inaugural Austin Championship . Chad Ramey, Erik van Rooyen and Sami Valimaki all could have shared the lead heading into Sunday's final round at Fazio Canyons Golf Course if Crowe had faltered down the stretch. But the 30-year-old Crowe, who is seeking his first win on Tour this week in Texas, birdied the par-3 17th and followed it up with another circle at No. 18 as part of the final grouping on the course. "It was like 220 straight into the wind, I was just trying to hit a 4-iron as low as I could and push it just a touch," Crowe recalled. "It was actually a pretty good shot to end up in that bunker, it was a good leave. He called the lie perfect as it was just sitting uphill. "It just came out perfect and went in — me and my caddie both had a feeling I was going to make that before we got it, so it was pretty cool to see that go in," he added. Heavy winds began to impact players still on their back nines Saturday afternoon, and Crowe was no exception. After setting the course record on Thursday with an opening-round 62, Crowe bogeyed the first two holes on his back nine on Moving Day. Another square at the par-4 16th put his chances in doubt but the run of birdies at the end of his round vaulted him ahead for the solo lead. item.title: Italy player ratings vs Belgium: Pio Esposito scores and misses a penalty as Roberto Mancini's Azzurri miss out on Nations League quarter-finals
item.description: FBL-EUR-NATIONS-BEL-ITA - AFP Italy needed only a draw in Brussels to reach the Nations League quarter-finals, but a 4-1 defeat to Belgium sent them from first to third in Group A1. Francesco Pio Esposito gave the Azzurri the lead in the 11th minute, stretching to turn in Michael Kayode's cross for his 10th goal in 15 caps. The advantage did not last long. Maxim De Cuyper equalised in the 15th minute, Nathan Ngoy turned in a corner in the 22nd and Jeremy Doku danced through the Italy defence to make it 3-1 in the 26th, with Charles De Ketelaere setting up two of the three. Gianluigi Donnarumma kept the score down with a string of saves, and De Ketelaere also hit the bar, but Diego Moreira added a fourth in the 80th minute. Pio Esposito had the chance to reduce the deficit in stoppage time, only for Senne Lammens to save his penalty after VAR spotted a Nicolas Raskin handball. Belgium finished with 22 shots to Italy's 12 and go through with group winners France, while the Azzurri finish third but are safe from relegation. Here are the Italy player ratings from the King Baudouin Stadium... Goalkeeper & Defence Gianluigi Donnarumma (6/10): Made six saves to stop the scoreline getting even heavier, denying Kevin De Bruyne three times, including a superb stop onto the post in the 43rd minute, and keeping out a fierce Doku strike. Had little chance with the goals, but was booked for dissent in the 81st minute as frustration set in. Michael Kayode (6/10): Delivered the cross for Pio Esposito's opener and caused problems with his long throws early on. Spent much of the night trying to stop Doku, though, giving away three free-kicks against the Manchester City winger. Giorgio Scalvini (6/10): Helped Kayode deal with Doku in the first half, but became the second Italy player booked for bringing down the winger in the 51st minute. Made way for Alphadjo Cisse on 62 minutes as Mancini went in search of goals. Alessandro Bastoni (6/10): Pushed on to support Italy's early pressure down the left. Belgium appealed for a penalty when he grappled with De Cuyper in the box midway through the second half, but neither the referee nor VAR were interested, and he later cleared a De Ketelaere cross away from the lurking Doku. Riccardo Calafiori (5/10): Teed up Nicolo Fagioli for one of Italy's best early chances, but Belgium's equaliser came from Timothy Castagne's cut-back down his side. item.title: Smyth scores 55-yard field goal in Saints defeat
item.description: Smyth was making his second NFL appearance of the season against the Panthers [Getty Images] Kicker Charlie Smyth landed a late 55-yard field goal, but it wasn't enough to stop New Orleans Saints falling to a 20-17 defeat against Carolina Panthers on Sunday. The former Gaelic footballer, from Mayobridge in County Down, was making his second NFL appearance of the season after being elevated from the practice squad for a second successive week. The 25-year-old helped the Saints to an overtime win against Cleveland Browns last weekend with three field goals and two extra points and he was almost the hero again against the Panthers. Smyth, who also kicked two extra points, landed a 55-yard field goal with just 41 seconds left in regulation time to tie the game at 17-17. However, Panthers quarterback Bryce Young's drive set up Panthers' kicker Ryan Fitzgerald to score a 54-yard field goal on the final play to win the game.

item.title: ‘Hitting the Powerball’… Kansas City Chiefs star has never had it so good, says Ryan Clark
item.description: Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs’ newest receiving weapon showed up immediately against the Atlanta Falcons. Chiefs general manager Brett Veach provided a surprise for quarterback Patrick Mahomes at the NFL trade deadline, agreeing a trade for Josh Downs. Downs was traded away by the Indianapolis Colts to the Chiefs for a fourth and fifth round pick, a move that could end up looking like a bargain. The new Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver made an instant impact in Week 10 in his first game for his new team. Downs caught his first touchdown from Patrick Mahomes in the second quarter, catching an 18-yard pass in the endzone. NFL expert Ryan Clark reacted to Downs’ first Chiefs touchdown by reflecting on the incredible turnaround in fortunes for the receiver – after leaving the 2-7 Colts. Clark posted on social media: “Man, imagine going to sleep one week with Daniel Jones as your QB, and waking up the next with Patrick Mahomes! “That’s the football version of hitting the Powerball! I know Josh Downs feels like a new man!” Downs leaves a losing team for a winning team Josh Downs had requested a trade away from the Indianapolis Colts after their poor start to the season, and clear intention to rebuild. His Colts team were 2-7 heading into Week 10, while the Chiefs were 6-2 prior to their win over the Falcons. Downs has never played a game in the NFL Playoffs during his three seasons in Indianapolis. Now providing he can stay injury-free in Kansas City, Downs will likely finally get the chance to play in the postseason with the Chiefs. It’s hard to disagree with Ryan Clark’s assessment that he has ‘won the Powerball’ with the trade. item.title: Tuchel hails England’s biggest win under his management
item.description: Tuchel hails England’s biggest win under his management Thomas Tuchel has described England’s 3-2 victory over Spain as the best win of his reign as his side topped their Nations League group. England ended Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run in Madrid thanks to goals from Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White, despite playing the final half an hour with ten men after Elliot Anderson was sent off. Asked whether it was his best victory as England boss, Tuchel said: “Given the circumstances, against who and where we played, yeah.” The England manager compared the pressure his side faced late on to their World Cup meeting with Mexico at the Azteca. “It was like at the Azteca,” he said. “Against this team, half an hour feels like two hours. “Without the red card, I think we had a clear win.” Tuchel was particularly pleased with the mentality England demonstrated against the world champions. “What we’re made of, what we can do, that we trust the process and that we’re hungry enough to develop and always ready to push our limits,” he said when asked what his team showed. “We had the best result in 60 years at the World Cup and we were not happy with it and wanted to get better. “We bridged the gap and the things we wanted to improve, we did. “It’s impressive what we’ve done in the last two camps, so full credit to the team.”

item.title: Andreeva defeats Svitolina to win WTA Finals
item.description: Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva celebrates victory over Elina Svitolina in the WTA Finals in Indian Wells (MATTHEW STOCKMAN) Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva battled past Elina Svitolina in straight sets to win the season-ending WTA Finals crown on Sunday. Andreeva powered to a 7-5, 6-3 victory in a hard-fought duel in Indian Wells to complete a superb week in California. Reigning French Open champion Andreeva, 19, clinched the title without dropping a set in the tournament. She is only the third teenager after Chris Evert and Maria Sharapova to win the WTA Finals on their debut. "It feels amazing, of course I'm super-privileged to put my name in that group," said Andreeva. The teenager thanked friends, family and support staff in a victory speech, before light-heartedly thanking herself for her success. "I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work, for never quitting, for always believing in myself, for not taking the days off, for working every day, and for committing to what I have to do," said Andreeva, wearing a track-suit top with the slogan "I want to thank myself." A grueling 1hr 48min duel saw Andreeva secure a break in the opening game of the first set before holding for a 2-0 lead. Ukrainian veteran Svitolina broke back in the fourth game, conjuring a sublime angled volley to level at 2-2. Svitolina was soon back under pressure though, conceding another break to go 4-3 down before Andreeva held for a 5-3 lead. There was more drama to follow when Andreeva served for the first set at 5-4 up. She opened with back-to-back double faults to go 0-30 down, and then yanked a wild forehand wide to give Svitolina two break points at 15-40. A long forehand gave Svitolina the break to knot it at 5-5 but Andreeva hit back immediately with her third break of serve to regain the advantage at 6-5. The Russian made no mistake when serving for the set for a second time, holding comfortably to go 1-0 up. The second set followed a familiar pattern, with both players trading some brutal groundstrokes in a series of long rallies. Andreeva broke to take the lead at 1-0 but Svitolina responded in a marathon second game, breaking back after converting her seventh break point to level at 1-1. Andreeva edged back in front with a break to go 3-2 up and then held for a 4-2 lead. The next two games went with serve to leave Svitolina serving to stay in the match at 5-3 down. A fortunate net cord left Andreeva with three match points at 0-40. Svitolina saved the first and looked poised to save another, only to hit a wide open overhead smash into the net to give Andreeva the win. Svitolina, who had been thumped 6-4, 6-0 by Andreeva in the opening round-robin game of the tournament, took positives from her performance. "After the first match I was not expecting to play in the final," Svitolina said. "Unfortunately it didn't go my way but I gave it my all." rcw/amz

item.title: ‘So Happy for Him,’ ‘He’s What We Needed’ — NFL Fans React to Kirk Cousins Getting Emotional After Leading Minnesota to Huge Win vs. Packers
item.description: ‘So Happy for Him,’ ‘He’s What We Needed’ — NFL Fans React to Kirk Cousins Getting Emotional After Leading Minnesota to Huge Win vs. Packers Kirk Cousins had plenty of reasons to enjoy beating Green Bay, but getting through the postgame interview proved a little harder. Back in a Vikings uniform at the stadium where his first stint with Minnesota ended, Cousins became emotional discussing the road that brought him back. Fans who watched the moment were ready to welcome him home, even if this particular reunion happened on enemy territory. Kirk Cousins’ Return Hits Home With Vikings Fans Minnesota defeated the Packers 30-10 at Lambeau Field on Sunday, with Cousins completing 21 of 31 passes for 207 yards, two touchdowns, and an interception. item.title: Cucurella and Huijsen feature as Spain surrender Nations League group lead to England
item.description: MADRID, SPAIN - NOVEMBER 15: Jude Bellingham of England gestures towards Marc Cucurella of Spain during the UEFA Nations League 2026/27 group phase match between Spain and England at Riyadh Air Metropolitano on November 15, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. (Photo by Carl Recine/Getty Images) | Getty Images There was a party atmosphere at a sold-out Metropolitano on Sunday night as Spain hosted England in their first game in the Spanish capital since conquering the World Cup in the summer. Luis de la Fuente’s side had won five from five in the UEFA Nations League campaign and were unbeaten in 90 minutes in 43 games, since March 2024, with this expected to see them crowned as group winners in the UEFA Nations League. Instead, England ran out the winners, taking a 3-0 lead through a Harry Kane penalty, an Ezri Konsa header and a third from Ben White. Spain did battle back to 3-2 after the Three Lions went down to 10 men after Elliot Anderson was sent off for fouling Lamine Yamal in the box, with Mikel Oyarzabal scoring the resulting penalty and Nico Williams adding another. At left-back, Marc Cucurella had a night to forget. Booked for a foul on Morgan Rogers early in the second half, he won only one of five ground duels and didn’t complete any tackles as he struggled with the threat of Rogers down England’s right flank. Going forwards, he also contributed little with only two passes into the final third and failing to find his target with his only attempted cross. In the second half, he was joined by Dean Huijsen, who came on at the break to replace Pau Cubarsí, who conceded the penalty which gave England the lead before half-time. Huijsen too found it hard going up against Kane, losing all four of his aerial duels, and also failing to complete any tackles. Where he did contribute more was in Spain’s more direct approach with Huijsen often carrying the ball forwards before launching it into the final third later on, registering six passes into the final third and a step by 92% pass accuracy overall. Spain have now finished second in the group, behind England on goal difference, which means that they will face a tougher draw in the Nations League play-off before a final four.

item.title: The full Division III football bracket, along with at least 1 major snub
item.description: The transition from a selection committee to the NCAA Power Index (NPI) has taken some of the guess work from the Division III football championship bracket. The expansion from 32 teams to 40 has ensured fewer snubs. But that doesn't mean this year's field doesn't bring surprises. Geographic limitations and the NPI's difference of opinion with the D3Football.com rankings means there's plenty to quibble about with this year's schedule. Wheaton College, the first team to beat powerhouse North Central in the regular season since 2019, went from the poll's No. 1 team to the bracket's third overall seed. Wisconsin-Whitewater, chasing its first national title since 2014, will have home field advantage all the way to the national championship game in Salem, Virginia after topping out the NPI formula. Teams with solid resumes, like Bethel and reigning national champion Wisconsin-River Falls, were left out. The New England Small College Athletic Conference (NESCAC) put three teams in the bracket even though the league didn't play a single out-of-conference game . North Central and DePauw, each ranked in the poll's top 15, will face off in a second round game that ensures at least one realistic title contender will be gone before the field is whittled down to 16 teams. You can find the full bracket here . Or expand the image below. The tournament begins November 21. The national title will be decided, on January 3, on ESPN. What's the best second round matchup? Glad you asked! DePauw at North Central is the obvious call. But that only gives way to a slate of third round bangers. We could get another Mary Hardin-Baylor vs. Whitewater matchup, a test of Calvin's mettle against Wisconsin-Platteville and Saint John's against whomever wins that DePauw/North Central showdown. item.description: Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can When you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium. AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.” Continue reading...

item.title: De la Fuente feels the strain as Lamine Yamal club v country debate rages in Spain
item.description: Head coach hits out at ‘lies’ as suggestions of preferential treatment for young star overshadow preparations for England game in Madrid From the London Palladium to Madrid’s Metropolitano, they’re all here. On Sunday night, the footballers who lifted the game’s biggest awards meet again three weeks later and on the field this time, dinner jackets but not a single man left behind. Harry Kane, the Ballon d’Or and Gerd Müller trophy winner. Unai Simón, holder of the Lev Yashin award . Luis de la Fuente , the coach of the year who on Thursday night announced that also joining them will be Lamine Yamal , the kid who lifted the Kopa award as the best young player for the third year running and said he would have preferred Pau Cubarsí to be standing there instead. And, yes, Cubarsí will be there too for the final Nations League group game. At 1.45pm on Friday the world and European champions landed back at Madrid’s Barajas airport from Prague, where they had won again, before making their way by bus to their Las Rozas HQ, around the M40 motorway to the north-west of the capital. At about the same time, Lamine Yamal arrived from Barcelona, due in at midday. As was Mikel Oyarzabal , scorer of the winner at Euro 2024 and Spain’s top marksman this summer (not that he would ever tell you so) from San Sebastián. At 7.30pm, they trained, preparing to meet the World Cup semi-finalists and the team they defeated in Berlin at the end of Euro 2024. Two starters from the World Cup final will be absent: Dani Olmo and the captain, 2024 Ballon d’Or winner Rodri , are injured. But everyone else will be there. Continue reading...

item.title: Football Daily | Taking a brief minute to remember Pierre Sage’s impact at Crystal Palace
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! So farewell then, Pierre Sage . Many coaches leave under a cloud, not many have their departures completely obscured by the foul, retch-inducing one emanating from another team’s managerial circus, but such was Sage’s fate . The news section of Crystal Palace’s website helpfully tells you the amount of time it might take you to read each story it links through to. For example it should take four minutes or so to get through Tuesday’s “On this day: five big Crystal Palace birthdays”. “England: I love a knee slide!” will take you five. “Prize draw: be a mascot for our next [Bigger Vase] tie!” is a two-minute job. The statement informing the world of Sage’s exit? One minute. Eighty-three words. By way of illustration, the word “words” was the 84th of this paragraph. Just because the man’s French doesn’t mean his exit should be marked with a shrug. As I have been away at a conference, giving a presentation that the MC described as ‘sobering’, I’ve missed the last few days of football, so I was very sad to read about the passing of the great Danny Kelly . Others are far better placed to give tributes to the great man, but for younger generations who can’t comprehend the football cultural significance, Baker and Kelly represented the peak of football phone-ins. Before it became people ranting and raving about wanting the manager sacked as they’ve lost a few games or wanting the club to spend another few hundred million pounds on yet more players, it was about football supporters and supporting, from fans who actually went to games. Their peak was on BBC Radio in the 1990s, and there are too many examples of their greatness, but if I had to pick one, just one to illustrate it, it would, of course, be Gordon the Dundee United supporter and his bow tie . Rest in Peace, Danny Kelly. You gave us such joy” – Noble Francis. As they no longer seem to be ‘Dr Tottenham’, I was wondering if they had maybe passed the soubriquet on. I think the England cricket team has provided the answer (again)” – Andrew Parker. item.title: Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed
item.description: After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics Sign up for our free newsletter here Enzo Maresca seemed, if not quite baffled by his side’s Saturday defeat to Nottingham Forest, then at least a little put out. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances. In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. In the 1-0 home defeat to Brighton last weekend, they had 62% possession and 21 chances to seven. At the City Ground, it was 79% possession and 12 chances to 11. So Maresca is right in one way: City could look at basic statistics and say they had been unfortunate – although Forest could equally point to the fact that they went into that game third top of the expected goals table but second-bottom of the actual table. item.title: Felix Nmecha’s faith is forcing Borussia Dortmund into an uncomfortable debate
item.description: Midfielder’s spectacular strikes rescued a frustrating day, only for celebrations to reignite dialogue that has followed him through his career It was just what they needed at just the right time. item.title: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’
item.description: Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.” With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week. Continue reading...

item.description: Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. item.title: Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football
item.description: Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it. The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous? Continue reading...

item.description: The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times . That would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. item.description: It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. item.title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe
item.description: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out. Continue reading...

item.description: Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
